an0641.user: Amazon Ads is killing me. Skincare brand, AOV ₹1300, 40% margin. Six weeks ago CAC was ₹527 and ROAS 2.5, now CAC is ₹1041 and ROAS has fallen to 1.2. I think Amazon's algorithm changed on me or my targeting got messed up — same audience, same creatives the whole time. What did Amazon break?
an0641.assistant:
Amazon didn't break anything. You did the opposite of break it — you left everything exactly the same for six weeks, and that's the problem.

Look at what moved together: CAC doubled ₹527→₹1041, ROAS halved 2.5→1.2, CTR is sliding, frequency is sitting at 3.2. Same creatives, same audience. That pattern has one name — creative fatigue. Your buyers have seen the same ads enough times that they've stopped reacting, so Amazon has to show them more often (frequency up) to get the same click, and each conversion costs more. It's not the algorithm losing the plot; it's your creative aging out.

The cost of doing nothing: contribution is now ₹1300 × 40% − ₹1041 = ₹520 − ₹1041 = −₹521 per order. You're paying ₹521 to acquire each sale. Six weeks ago at ₹527 CAC you were roughly breakeven; the fatigue ate the whole cushion.

The lever: refresh the creative with genuinely new angles — different hook, different problem framing, not a recolour — and from now on run a testing cadence so you're never riding a single winner until it dies. Rotate before frequency climbs past ~2.5, not after.

One caveat: confirm the frequency and CTR slide are steady across the six weeks and not a festive-traffic blip. But same-creative + rising-frequency + falling-CTR is textbook — I'd start cutting new creatives today.

an0642.user: Wanted a sharper read on my Meesho Ads funnel before I touch anything. Footwear brand, last 30 days: 32,000 visits, 3,008 add-to-carts, 1,820 reached checkout, 470 purchases. CTR around 2%. The traffic feels fine but something downstream isn't converting and I can't see what. What's the non-obvious bit here?
an0642.assistant:
The non-obvious bit is that your acquisition is genuinely healthy and you're probably about to blame the wrong half of the funnel.

Walk it down. 3,008 carts on 32,000 visits is a 9.4% add-to-cart rate — that's a strong top of funnel; people want the product. 1,820 of them reached checkout, also fine. Then 470 purchase out of 1,820 who reached checkout — that's 26%. That's the number that should stop you. A healthy checkout→purchase sits around 50–70%. You're losing roughly three of every four people who've already pulled out their wallet and started checking out.

That's not an ad problem and it's not an interest problem — by checkout the intent is already proven. It's friction at the last step: a shipping cost that appears only at checkout, a forced account login, no UPI or COD option, an OTP that fails, a coupon field that taunts people into leaving to hunt for a code.

The lever: instrument the checkout. Add step-level drop-off tracking between reached-checkout and purchase, then go through it yourself on a cheap Android phone on mobile data and watch where it breaks. Your ad money is doing its job — leave the campaigns alone.

Caveat: 470 purchases is enough to trust the shape, but the 26% is a blended number — segment it by payment method and device, because the leak is usually concentrated in one (COD failing, or one payment rail timing out).

an0643.user: Okay I'm a bit panicked. B2B SaaS for CA firms, running WhatsApp broadcast plus search on broad-match keywords. Last 30 days I got 9.3 lakh impressions, 10,832 clicks, that's 1.2% CTR, and out of all that — 52 orders. Conversion rate 0.48%. AOV ₹1100. The reach is huge but almost nobody buys, I feel like I'm shouting into a void. Is my CTR too low?
an0643.assistant:
Breathe — your CTR isn't the problem, and chasing it would make this worse.

1.2% CTR on 9.3 lakh impressions giving you 10,832 clicks is perfectly normal. The number that actually explains your pain is the one right after it: 0.48% conversion. Ten thousand people clicked and 52 bought. When clicks are plentiful but conversion is a rounding error, you're not buying the wrong volume — you're buying the wrong intent.

The cause is sitting in your setup: broad-match keywords. Broad match sprays you across loosely related searches, so you're paying for people who are browsing, curious, comparing — not CA firms actively shopping for your software. They click because the ad is relevant enough to be interesting, then bounce because they were never in-market. High reach, low intent. That's a CA-firm tool being shown to people who run a kirana shop's accounts on a notebook.

The lever: tighten intent. Move to phrase/exact match on the searches a CA firm actually types when they want what you sell, pile on negative keywords to cut the tyre-kickers, and stop optimising the campaign for clicks — optimise for the action that costs you money downstream.

Caveat: 52 orders is a thin base to draw a hard conclusion, so don't slash the account in one move. Pull your search-terms report first — you'll likely see the budget bleeding into a handful of junk broad-match queries, and killing those is the fastest win.

an0644.user: Calm read please, not a panic. Jewellery brand, doing about ₹16L a month, last 90 days steady. Roughly 95% of that revenue comes through Meta, everything else combined is maybe 5%. 95% of ₹16L a month rides on a single platform you don't control. That's ₹15.2L of monthly revenue sitting on one ad account, one algorithm, one set of policy rules. This isn't a numbers-are-bad read; every number you have is good. It's a concentration-risk read. The proving number is the 95% itself: there is no shock absorber. A jewellery brand with healthy economics on Meta is exactly the kind of account that gets flagged, because the category trips a lot of automated filters.

The lever: stand up a genuine second channel now — while you're choosing to, with cashflow and patience, not when Meta forces you to. For jewellery I'd test Google (high-intent search for what you sell) or a real organic/WhatsApp retention motion off your existing buyers, so some revenue stops depending on the auction entirely.

Caveat: don't yank budget off Meta to fund this — it's working. Fund the second channel as additive insurance and judge it on its own breakeven, not against Meta's mature efficiency.

an0645.user: IELTS edtech, blended Meta + Google. Pasting the numbers, tell me what's wrong. AOV ₹1450, gross margin 57%. Eight weeks ago I was spending ₹4.5L/mo, CAC ₹650, ROAS 2.2. I pushed spend up to ₹9.9L to grow faster and now CAC is ₹913 and ROAS dropped to 1.6. More money, worse numbers. What broke?
an0645.assistant:
Nothing broke. You hit the ceiling of the audience you had, and the extra budget is buying the people who were never going to convert as cheaply.

Here's the mechanic. You more than doubled spend, ₹4.5L→₹9.9L. The best-intent IELTS searchers and lookalikes — the ones who were already costing you ₹650 — are a finite pool, and you'd mostly bought them at ₹4.5L. The marginal rupee after that doesn't find more cheap buyers; it reaches colder, more expensive people. So CAC drifts ₹650→₹913 and ROAS slides 2.2→1.6. That's not failure, that's saturation. The channel has an efficient ceiling and you found it.

Watch what it did to contribution. At ₹650 CAC: ₹1450 × 57% − ₹650 = ₹826.5 − ₹650 = +₹176.5 per enrolment, comfortable. At ₹913: ₹826.5 − ₹913 = −₹86.5. The incremental spend dragged you from profitable into the red.

The lever: you can't fix this by pushing harder into the same pool. You have to create new demand before you add more budget — new audiences, new creative angles for different aspirant segments (study-abroad vs immigration vs band-score-stuck), a new channel like YouTube or organic. Scale the surface area, then the budget.

Caveat: confirm the CAC rise tracks the spend ramp week-by-week and isn't an IELTS exam-cycle seasonal lull — both look similar on a chart, but only one is fixed by widening the funnel.

an0646.user: Quick one — why is my CTR low? Selling on Amazon, last 30 days: AOV ₹1850, 60% margin, CAC ₹542, ROAS 3.4, CTR 1.3%. The CTR's been bugging me, feels like it should be higher.
an0646.assistant:
Your CTR is fine — leave it alone. 1.3% on Amazon Ads is normal, and you're asking about the one number that isn't your problem.

Look at the rest: ROAS 3.4, CAC ₹542. First-order contribution is ₹1850 × 60% − ₹542 = ₹1110 − ₹542 = +₹568 per order. Acquisition is genuinely working — you're buying a profitable first sale every time. So why am I not telling you to scale?

Because of the number you didn't ask about: 90-day repeat is 8%. That's the leak. Out of every 100 buyers, 92 never come back. A model like this only works long-term if first-order profit compounds into a second and third order — that's where the real LTV lives. At 8% repeat, there's barely a second order, so your lifetime value is essentially your first-order contribution and nothing more. You're filling a bucket that has no bottom; pour more spend in and it just runs out faster.

The lever: fix repeat before you touch spend. Build the post-purchase motion — a replenishment nudge on WhatsApp timed to when the product runs out, a reason and a reminder to reorder. Get that 8% moving first.

Caveat: 8% over 90 days can be partly category-driven (some products genuinely have long repurchase cycles). Check what your honest replenishment window is before you decide how broken it is — but on these numbers, retention is the constraint, not CTR.

an0647.user: No-code SaaS, mostly selling through email. Numbers roughly: average order around ₹1250, my gross margin's about 32%, CAC is ₹653, ROAS sits at 1.9, email CTR 2.1%. My real question is how do I bring my CAC down — it feels too high for what I'm selling.

You're aiming at the wrong target. CAC isn't your disease; it's a symptom of a margin that can't carry it.

Do the contribution math: ₹1250 × 32% − ₹653 = ₹400 − ₹653 = −₹253 per order. Even if you were a genius at ads and clawed CAC down ₹100, you'd still be at −₹153. A 32% gross margin is just too thin to fund customer acquisition through paid channels — there isn't enough gross profit left after COGS to pay for the sale, no matter how clean the targeting is. The proving number is the 32% itself, sitting under a healthy-looking 2.1% CTR. The email is doing its job; the economics underneath it aren't.

The lever: this is a margin problem wearing a marketing costume. Fix the gross margin before you touch the ads — get COGS down (infra/hosting/support cost per account), raise price, or lift AOV with an annual plan or a higher tier. Every point of margin you add does more for contribution than any CAC tweak. Get margin into the 60%+ range a SaaS should run at, then ₹653 CAC becomes comfortable.

Caveat: 32% is unusually low for software — if it's inflated by heavy support or onboarding cost, that may be a packaging/self-serve fix rather than a pricing one. Pin down what's actually eating the 68% first.

an0648.user: Home-care D2C, blended Meta + Google. My conversion rate dropped 9% this week versus last week — only had about 50 conversions this week. I'm thinking of overhauling the whole funnel and creative strategy this weekend. Where do I start?
an0648.assistant:
You start by not doing that. Close the laptop.

A 9% move in conversion rate on a base of 50 conversions is noise, not a trend. At 50 conversions, a handful of orders either way swings your rate by more than 9% — that's normal week-to-week variance, the statistical equivalent of a coin landing heads a few extra times. There's no signal in it to act on, and overhauling your funnel and creative off one wobbly week is exactly how founders whipsaw their accounts into a worse place than they started.

Do nothing this weekend. What would actually count as a real shift: the same direction holding for 3–4 consecutive weeks, or a single move big enough to clear the noise on this base — think a 25–30%+ drop, not 9%. Until then you're reading static.

If the itch is unbearable, spend the weekend setting up clean weekly tracking and a bigger sample so next time you can tell a signal from a coin flip — not rebuilding things that aren't broken.

If you want to do something useful, lengthen your reporting window to a trailing 4-week average so the noise stops triggering you — that's the fix here, not the targeting.
